sure.title: How sure are we?
sure.tagline: What radar does well, where it struggles, and what this is.
sure.agreement.pending: Agreement scores are computed at the event by comparing our maps with NASA's water maps. Each will show a range and a one-line meaning.
sure.f1.gloss: How well the two maps agree on water, from 0 to 1.
sure.iou.gloss: Share of all water pixels that both maps call water. Copernicus GFM aims for 0.70 or more.
sure.offset.gloss: Days between our radar picture and NASA's.
sure.benchmark: For scale: NISAR's mission target for flooded area is 80% accuracy at 1 ha every 12 days. That is a goal, not a result we have shown.
sure.values.title: Typical radar values
sure.values.tagline: Numbers appear only with a source, or measured from our own scenes at the event.
values.water.vv: Very dark; at or below −15.5 dB (an operational tool's upper limit)
values.water.vh: Very dark; at or below −23 dB (same tool)
lim.provisional: Provisional data. NISAR passes before 21 Oct 2026 are PROVISIONAL: calibrated, but validated only at a few sites, none in Southeast Asia. NASA publishes validated NISAR products from 21 Oct 2026. Treat every number as an estimate.
lim.revisit.ked: Revisit gaps. Each NISAR track passes every 12 days, so short floods can be missed. There is no NISAR data from 27 Jul to 10 Aug 2026.
lim.revisit.kel: Revisit gaps. In late 2024 only one Sentinel-1 satellite was working, so Kelantan was seen about every 6 days.
lim.nonisarflood: No NISAR flood yet. NISAR began in mid-2026 and has not yet seen a Malaysian monsoon flood. The 2024 Kelantan flood is shown with Sentinel-1 radar (C-band, NASA OPERA products).
lim.blind.kel: Radar blind spots. Radar can confuse calm water with smooth roads, sand or radar shadow, and may miss water in dense towns or under thick canopy, where flooded streets can look bright. Wind and rain can roughen water.
lim.blind.ked: Radar blind spots. Radar can confuse calm water with smooth surfaces such as dry farmland, smooth soil or radar shadow. Wind and rain can roughen water.
lim.schedule: Paddy schedule. Planting dates come from a MADA notice and may differ field by field, especially in the 2026 drought year. The schedule is not observed planting.
lim.choices.kel: Our choices. On every date the Otsu threshold came out above HydroSAR's −15.5 dB VV ceiling, so we used −15.5 dB. Moving it 1 dB lower gives the low end of the range shown. No slope or HAND masks are applied, and towns are flagged rather than mapped, so our flood areas are a lower bound.
lim.choices.ked: Our choices. Water thresholds come from Otsu on cropland, on the most clearly two-peaked date of each NISAR stack, and are applied to all dates of that stack. HydroSAR's caps are for C-band, so none is applied. Moving both thresholds by ±1 dB gives the range shown. Cropland = ESA WorldCover 2021.
lim.notwarning: Not a warning service. This is not an official warning. For live river levels see Public InfoBanjir (JPS). For evacuation follow NADMA, JKM and APM instructions.
lim.notwarning.short: Not a warning service. Check MADA for planting advice.
lim.notreviewed: Not reviewed. This is a student hackathon prototype using NASA data. It has not been reviewed or endorsed by NASA or by outside scientists.
lim.passdays: Radar only on pass days. Radar maps exist only on days the satellite passed over. Days in between have no radar picture; we do not fill them in.
lim.imagery: Imagery only. Explore anywhere shows NASA's ready-made radar pictures. They are not measurements, and the NISAR pictures are provisional. Different land covers can look alike.
lim.falsealarm.kel: False alarms and misses. Floods can be missed in towns, under thick trees, and when wind or heavy rain roughens the water as the satellite passes. Smooth roads and sand can be wrongly marked as water.
lim.falsealarm.ked: False alarms and misses. Europe's Copernicus flood service warns that farmland can look like flood water to radar, depending on how crops are grown. In Kedah that is partly what we want to see, but smooth dry soil can also look wet.

story.1.title: Radar sees through cloud
story.1.body: During the monsoon, Kelantan can be under cloud for days. Radar satellites bring their own signal, so they see the ground anyway.
story.2.title: 17 November 2024: before
story.2.body: A normal radar view of the Kelantan delta. Rivers and lakes are dark because calm water reflects the signal away.
story.3.title: 29 November 2024: the flood
story.3.body: Twelve days later, on the steep rise toward the peak, large areas have filled with water. Drag the slider to compare the two dates.
story.4.title: Where it hit
story.4.body: Our radar map counts new flood water district by district: tap a row to see where it hit. On 29 Nov, Pasir Mas and Tumpat had the most evacuees.
story.5.title: Kedah: NISAR watches fields fill
story.5.bridge: Same radar physics: dark = smooth water. In Kelantan it showed a disaster. In Kedah it shows farmers at work.
story.5.body: NISAR's longer L-band radar looked at Kedah's paddies every few days from 23 September to 1 November 2026.
story.6.title: How sure are we?
story.6.body: We compare our maps with NASA's water maps. In Kedah that is a different radar; in Kelantan it only checks consistency. Not reviewed by NASA.
story.6.global: NISAR scans nearly all of Earth's land twice every 12 days, so this works far beyond Malaysia.

about.title: About the data
about.tagline: Where every picture and number comes from.
about.passdays.title: Why only some days have radar
about.passdays.body: A radar satellite does not watch one place all the time. It takes a picture of a strip of ground as it flies over, and comes back to the same strip on the same path every 12 days. In late 2024 only one Sentinel-1 satellite was working, and it crossed Kelantan on two paths, so the area was seen about every 6 days. Between 17 and 29 November 2024 there are only three radar pictures: 17, 24 (early morning) and 29 November. On the other days there is simply no radar picture. We do not fill the gaps with guesses.
about.challenge.title: The challenge asks… our answer
about.why.a: Kelantan: rain is the trigger (monsoon surges and low-pressure systems), the landscape is the amplifier, and high tides slow drainage of the flat delta. Kedah: people flood fields on a schedule set by dam water and rain; in 2026, drought changed that schedule.
about.pol.a: HH for open water and double bounce (flooded towns and forest, early paddy); HV for crop growth and canopy. Sentinel-1's VV and VH play the same roles at C-band.
about.future.a: Flood extent for disaster teams every 12 days per track, a rice planting-progress monitor for MADA, and drought-season irrigation checks, for any river or rice granary NISAR covers.
about.credits.title: Data and credits
about.granules.note: Pinned by pipeline/01_search.py; the full list is in data/manifest/ when the pipeline is run.
about.ai.title: How AI was used
about.ai.body: This app was written with Claude Code (Anthropic) from the team's plan. The focus-area summaries in the AI analysis dashboard are drafts written by Claude from the plan's sourced facts; they are not yet reviewed, and radar figures in them come only from our pipeline. In the refined version, AI writes the summaries at build time, code fills every number from our radar maps, and a person checks them. There is no AI running in the page. All AI use is disclosed in AI_USAGE.md.

gloss.sar: SAR: a satellite radar that sends microwave pulses sideways and records the echoes. Works day or night, through cloud.
gloss.backscatter: Backscatter: the part of the radar signal that bounces back. Weak = dark pixel; strong = bright pixel.
gloss.hhhv: HH / HV: first letter = sent, second = received. HH shows water best; HV shows plants.
gloss.band: L-band / C-band: NISAR's 24 cm waves reach deeper into plants than Sentinel-1's ~5.5 cm waves.
gloss.pass: Pass day: a day the satellite flew over and took a radar picture.
gloss.track: Track: the repeating path of a satellite pass. Same-track pairs compare fairly.

live.body: The north-east monsoon usually brings Kelantan's floods between November and January. NISAR began its science mission in 2026, so this is the first monsoon it can watch here. This view reads NASA's newest pictures directly, with no processing of ours.

explain.title: How radar sees water
explain.tagline: Four kinds of echo explain the colours on this map.
explain.mirror.title: Calm water is a mirror.
explain.mirror.body: The wave glances off away from the satellite, so almost nothing returns. Water looks dark in every channel.
explain.rough.title: Rough ground and choppy water.
explain.rough.body: The wave scatters in all directions and some comes back. VV and HH show this best. Wind or rain on water makes it brighter, which can hide a flood.
explain.volume.title: Leaves and branches.
explain.volume.body: The wave bounces around inside the canopy and comes back twisted. Cross-pol (HV, VH) rises as crops and trees grow.
explain.double.title: Double bounce.
explain.double.body: Water, then a wall, trunk or rice stem, sends the wave straight back. HH is brightest here, so flooded forest, flooded towns and young paddy can look bright, not dark.
explain.c: Sentinel-1 (about 5.5 cm): the Kelantan flood and NASA OPERA maps. Mostly sees the top of plants.
explain.s: NISAR's second radar (ISRO, about 10 cm). Not used here.
explain.l: NISAR (about 24 cm): Kedah's paddies. Reaches stems and trunks, so it sees water under plants better.

sure.agreement.kel: Scored on land only. At the flood peak, 29 Nov 2024: F1 {f1}, IoU {iou}. On dry dates there is little water on land, so a few river edges decide the score and it is low. The storm-roughened sea on 29 Nov looked bright to the radar, so the sea is left out.
sure.agreement.ked: NISAR finds far more field water than NASA's C-band map. Almost all of NASA's water is inside ours, but most of ours is not in NASA's. Either L-band sees shallow paddy water that C-band misses, or smooth tilled soil looks like water at L-band. Without checks on the ground we cannot tell which. See the layer 'Where NISAR and Sentinel-1 disagree'.
